workstreams.name: Foundation
workstreams.description: Project scaffolding and the seams everything else plugs into: electron-vite build, Vue 3 + Nuxt UI standalone renderer, the typed IPC contract in src/shared, context-isolated preload, lint/test baseline and CI. Owns the answer to R4 (Nuxt UI standalone integration, unverified).

workstreams.name: Library
workstreams.description: Everything main-process and on-disk: schema v1 and migrations, root folders, recursive scanner, music-metadata parsing, incremental mtime rescan, filesystem watcher, artwork thumbnail cache, FTS5 index, background job queue. Owns R3 (inotify limits) and the relative-path portability rule.

workstreams.name: Audio
workstreams.description: The Web Audio graph and everything scheduled through it: AudioEngine interface, decodeAudioData implementation, prefetch and sample-accurate scheduling, gapless, crossfade, ReplayGain application. Owns R1 (decode memory ceiling) and R2 (gapless/crossfade exclusivity) — the two risks most likely to force architectural change.

workstreams.name: UI
workstreams.description: The three-pane shell and its panel islands: Sources, TrackList, NowPlaying. Virtualized lists from the first commit, sortable configurable columns, shift/ctrl multi-select, transport controls, and the CSS custom-property token layer that makes theming structural rather than bolted on.

workstreams.name: Packaging and Ops
workstreams.description: electron-builder targets (NSIS on Windows, AppImage + deb on Linux), GitHub Actions matrix across windows-latest and ubuntu-latest, and the library export/import bundle that carries playlists, ratings and play counts between machines (D11).

workstreams.name: Playlists and Queue
workstreams.description: Playlist tabs as the backbone plus the transient play-next queue layered on top (D5). Owns the seven queue-semantics rules in design section 5 and their tests, fractional-position reordering, and m3u8 export. The interaction between tabs and queue is the specified surface most likely to grow bugs.

workstreams.name: Tunedeck
workstreams.description: The extended control and information surface (D15): a resizable right-side drawer hosting a panel island, opened from NowPlaying. Phase 1 (M5) is entirely local — up-next queue editor, format and signal readout, play history trail, related-in-library. Phase 2 (M7) is the artist nexus and Oscine's first network surface: D14's opt-in consent gate, a main-process-only fetch layer against MusicBrainz and Wikipedia, cache.db with TTLs and negative caching, and R5's artist identity resolution with operator correction. Owns D14, D15 and R5.

workstreams.name: Settings
workstreams.description: The configuration substrate the rest of development builds on. A declarative registry in src/shared/settings.ts is the single source of truth: every key declares type, default, scope, version, validator, control hint, label, help text and search keywords, and the settings surface is generated from it — adding a setting is a one-line entry, not UI work. Two backing stores read the registry: a main-process SQLite `settings` table for `durable` keys (audio, library, theme, anything main must read before the window opens, anything that belongs in the D11 export) and a single localStorage backend for `view` keys (pane sizes, open tabs, column widths — machine-local session state that must not pay an IPC round-trip per drag). Absorbs the five independently hand-rolled localStorage modules that exist today. Values resolve through a cascade — global then per-entity override — formalizing what playlists.setCrossfade already does ad hoc. Writes apply immediately and broadcast across IPC; nothing is staged behind OK/Cancel. Per-key versioned migrations, and unknown keys are preserved rather than dropped, so branch-switching does not destroy an operator's settings. Owns theme selection and operator-authored token overrides (W4 owns the token layer itself), settings export/import, and first-run onboarding. Does NOT own the D14 network consent gate (W7) or a keyboard-shortcut subsystem — the latter is currently homeless and needs a home before remapping can be offered.

workstreams.name: Podcasts
workstreams.description: Subscriptions to remote feeds as a domain parallel to the library rather than an extension of it (D16): migration 005's `podcasts` and `episodes` tables, main-process RSS and OPML parsing, byte-capped stall-guarded downloads into a machine-local podcasts directory, and playback of episodes from disk through the existing `oscine:` protocol on its own hostname and id space. No episode is ever a row in `tracks`, so Library facets, `tracks_fts` and ReplayGain stay music-only. Owns the Podcasts view — subscription rail, show tabs, virtualized episode list — and Discover, which queries the keyless Apple iTunes catalogue for search, genre charts and recommendation shelves. Shares exactly two things with W2: the artwork thumbnail cache with its single worker, and the custom protocol. Does NOT own the D14 consent gate (W7-6); Discover currently reaches Apple ahead of it, which is recorded debt rather than a settled position.

workstreams.name: Listening
workstreams.description:
The durable record of what was actually listened to, and everything local that reads it. Owns D17 (the uncapped, snapshot-carrying `listens` log) and D18 (favorites as a table of truth with a pinned playlist as its face), migrations 012–014, and D11's amendment carrying the log across machines. Specified in the wiki page `fermata-listening-and-scrobbling`.

Two records coexist and must not be confused. `play_history` (migration 009, W7-4) stays exactly as it is: 500 rows, skips included, written at transport-commit, excluded from the export bundle — the transport's short-term memory, so jump-back has somewhere to go. `listens` is the long-term one: uncapped, append-only, written at *departure* only when Last.fm's threshold was crossed (>30s track, and half its duration or four minutes of accumulated *audible* time), carrying the real milliseconds listened. A skipped track produces a trail row and no listen.

This stream is the card that finally owns `tracks.play_count` and `tracks.last_played_at`, which migration 001 created and `src/shared/history.ts` has deliberately left unwritten ever since. They become maintained caches of the log, regenerable by full aggregation — which is precisely the condition D11's amendment named as its revisit trigger.

The load-bearing schema detail is `listens.track_id INTEGER REFERENCES tracks(id) ON DELETE SET NULL` with title/artist/album/genre snapshotted onto every row. Migration 009 records that a file moved between roots reads as a delete plus an insert; the trail can afford to lose rows to that and years of listening cannot.

Also owns genre normalization (`track_genres`, split and casefolded off the free-text `tracks.genre` column), the stats engine — one query shape over four dimensions — the Tunedeck's favorites and play-count panes, and the Listening dashboard. The dashboard is a dashboard, not a retrospective; a Wrapped-style year-in-review is W10-13 and is deliberately unspecified.

Does NOT own anything that opens a socket. That is W11.

workstreams.name: Scrobbling
workstreams.description:
Everything that leaves the machine on the strength of a listen. Owns D19 (shipped app key, per-user session key, provider-abstracted), migration 015's outbox, the Last.fm client, and the one-way push of favorites to Loved. Specified in the wiki page `fermata-listening-and-scrobbling`.

D14 rejected last.fm and §11 listed scrobbling as out of scope for v1, and D19 is the argument for why this is a new decision rather than a reopened one: D14 was scoping keyless read-only *metadata* sources for the artist nexus, where an API key buys nothing MusicBrainz gives away. A scrobble is a per-user authenticated *write*, and the operator signs into their own account before a byte leaves the machine. Read D19 before touching this stream — the distinction is the whole basis for its existence.

The two credentials do different jobs and must not be conflated. The `api_key` and shared secret identify the application, ship in the bundle, are extractable from the asar, and can scrobble for nobody on their own; an operator can override them with their own pair. The **session key** identifies the human, is obtained once per install through Last.fm's desktop flow, never expires, lives in Electron `safeStorage` (currently unused anywhere in `src/`), never crosses IPC after it is written, and never enters the settings table or D11's bundle.

Scrobbling deliberately sits **outside** D14's consent gate (W7-6). Typing your own password into your own account's login page is stronger consent than a checkbox naming a service, and nothing outbound happens until it completes. This is the opposite of the Podcast Discover debt.

Depends on W7 for reuse, not for permission: by M7 the main-process fetch layer, `NetFailureKind`, `NetResult<T>` and cancel-by-scope already exist, so the scrobble client is a client rather than a second HTTP stack. `NET_SCOPES` grows `'scrobble'`.

The outbox is the part most likely to grow bugs and it gets its own card and its own tests. Persist first and submit second, always, even when online — a scrobble that exists only in flight is one lost to a closed laptop lid.

workstreams.name: Discover
workstreams.description:
Curate's Discover pane: named local SQL recipes over the library and the listens log (D20). Nine 1.0 shelves, 5–10 playable items each, nothing fetched, nothing pinned to the rail. Specified in the wiki page `fermata-discover-1-0`.

Faces forward — what to play next from files already owned — where W10's dashboard faces backward. Does not call `stats.query` or `related.ts`; those engines answer different questions. Does not fire D18's revisit trigger: shelves are ephemeral recipes, and save-as-playlist produces an ordinary D12 row.

Does NOT own Podcast Discover (W9), the Listening dashboard (W10-12), MusicBrainz similar-artists (W7), or a Recently Added rail fixture.

workstreams.name: Quick Access
workstreams.description:
Instant keyboard-first navigation and quick access. Two features on one new substrate, specified in the wiki page `fermata-quick-access` (owns D21–D27, migration 016).

The **command palette** (D21) is a Nuxt UI `UCommandPalette` in a modal, global via Ctrl/Cmd+K and a title-bar affordance, that fuzzy-finds any view/album/artist/playlist/track/subscribed-show and runs the top actions — play, queue, play next, jump-to-a-setting, download the latest episode of a podcast. Blended grouped results by default; `>`/`@`/`#`/`/` prefixes narrow the mode. The palette is stateless (D22): actions fire-and-forget with a toast and their progress lives in the owning panel. The **Quick Menu** (D26) is a left-edge `UDrawer` on Now Playing holding three computed lists — Favorite Playlists, Recent Additions, Favorite Artists — left-side to stay clear of the Tunedeck.

Three new pieces of foundation are why this is one stream: a unified `search.query` channel (D23) — today only `tracks` are indexed via `tracks_fts`; favorites beyond tracks (D24), adding `playlist_favorites` and `artist_favorites` as per-entity tables mirroring D18's `track_favorites`, denoted by a **star** vs the track **heart**; and the arrival clock `tracks.indexed_at` (D25), stamped on insert and never on rescan-upsert — the exact column W12 recorded-debt #1 sketched, which this stream delivers and W12's future "Just arrived" recipe reads.

Does NOT reopen D18 (the drawer's Recent Additions is a computed list, not a pinned collection — see the D18 amendment), does NOT build W8's homeless keyboard-shortcut subsystem (D27 ships one binding as a seam W8 absorbs), and does NOT reach Apple's catalogue (D23/D14 — the palette is local; catalogue search stays in W9). Integrates W5 (queue/play activation) and W9 (podcast downloads) without duplicating either.

workstreams.name: Polish
workstreams.description:
The cross-cutting refinement pass that turns the milestone build into a 1.0: podcast QoL, navigation and Now Playing lifecycle, two power-user Interface toggles, the first (fixed) keyboard-shortcut set, title-menu View/Help with About and Open-Source modals, and editorial/tooltip/context-menu consistency sweeps. Specified in the wiki page `1-0-polish-and-qol`, which records the settled 2026-08-25 design decisions each card references (P1–P4, G1–G10, B1).

Owns no new schema or process boundary — it reaches across W4 (UI shell, tab nav, Now Playing bar, context menus), W8 (Interface settings for the auto-show and visibility toggles), W9 (podcast show page and subscription rail), W10 (the Listening->Stats rename and its scroll bug), and W13 (the Command Palette affordance the toggle governs, and the shortcut seam D27 sketched). Depends on those streams for reuse and surface, not for permission.

Deliberately does NOT build a rebindable keyboard-shortcut subsystem (G6 ships a fixed set; remapping is post-1.0 and still belongs to W8), and does NOT extend the context-menu pass to podcast episodes or rail items (G8 scope is track rows and album/artist cards only).

workstreams.name: Tagging
workstreams.description:
Free-form user tagging: the operator's own labels on tracks, applied app-side and surfaced through Tunedeck, with genre suggestions from the network behind D14's consent gate.

Two layers that must not be confused. The **file layer** — `tracks.genre` and the derived `track_genres` (split-and-casefolded, owned by W10) — stays exactly as it is: read-only, rebuilt from the tag on every rescan-upsert, the origin a chip is marked as coming from. The **user layer** is new: a `tags` vocabulary plus a `track_tags` join, applied by the operator, that survives rescan and never touches disk. Honouring D7 (v1 never writes tags to file) is the whole reason the user layer is app-side rather than a mutation of `tracks.genre`; it is not a reopening of D7 but a compliance with it. Should a later milestone add opt-in write-back, the `track_tags` rows with `source='user'` are precisely the diff to flush.

Genre and user tags are one free-form surface, not two taxonomies: file genres render as read-only origin-marked chips beside editable user tags, unified on the same casefold key `track_genres` already uses, so "Hip-Hop" and "hip hop" are one label across both.

The suggestion path is Oscine's use of what W7 already built. MusicBrainz returns `genres[]`/`tags[]` (vote-weighted) on artist and release-group entities but the integration does not fetch them today; adding that parse and routing it through `CacheService.through` with its own TTL inherits D14 for free — suggestions behave like Biography and Members (present online or warm, silently absent otherwise) while the local tag editor keeps working. Nothing is auto-applied: a suggestion is a claim about the world, and accepting one writes a `track_tags` row with `source='suggested'`, the same visible-and-correctable stance R5 takes on identity. MB tags are per-artist and per-release-group, so a suggestion applies to the track by default and offers a batch apply to the whole album or everything by the artist.

Depends on W2 (schema/scanner), W10 (owns `track_genres` normalization this extends), W7 (Tunedeck registry and the D14 net/cache layer) and W4 (TrackList column) for reuse and surface, not for permission. Does NOT write to disk (D7), does NOT reopen D7 or D14, and does NOT build a separate tag taxonomy divorced from genre.

workstreams.name: Tag Write-Back
workstreams.description:
The opt-in flush of app-side metadata corrections into the source audio files — the last major feature gated before a 1.0 release candidate. Owns decision D28 and executes the revisit trigger that D7 deferred: write-back was always roadmapped as an explicit opt-in once a test corpus and atomic-write handling existed, and this stream is that trigger firing (not a reopening of D7). Design authority is the wiki page `oscine-tag-writeback`.

The operator problem: bad genres and other junk tags live in the files. The app-side layers (W10's `track_genres`, W15's `track_tags`, D7's `track_overrides`) correct what the operator sees, but a library wipe or a move to a new machine re-scans the same remote files and the junk returns. Correcting the index without correcting the source is a treadmill; integrity has to reach the source.

D28 is a hybrid: the correction layers stay the live, instant, reversible working surface, and a distinct operator-initiated action computes a diff from them and writes it into the file tags — staged behind a review gate, backed up, applied atomically per file (temp-write + fsync + rename, audio stream bytes untouched), verified on read-back, and reported per file with one file's failure never aborting the batch. Nothing writes to disk implicitly, on edit, or on scan. Immediate per-edit writes and sidecar files were both rejected (see the doc).

Full tag surface in scope, phased so genre pain ships first and artwork/custom frames last: core text tags (title/artist/album/track/disc/genre/year), a library-wide genre canonicalization/alias engine unified on W15's casefold key, embedded artwork (APIC / METADATA_BLOCK_PICTURE), and round-tripped custom frames. Codec coverage is the v1 set only — flac | mp3 | vorbis | opus | aac; the engine refuses anything else rather than guessing.

Owns new risks R6 (tag-write corruption — the one operation that can destroy an operator's file) and R7 (out-of-band file drift), and the D7 preconditions as cards: W16-3 test corpus and W16-2/W16-4 atomic-write + rollback. Depends on W2 (schema/scanner), W15 (user tag layer = the diff), W10 (`track_genres`), W4 (review UI surface) for reuse and surface, not for permission. Library selection (leading candidate: pure-JS `node-taglib-sharp`, to avoid a third native-ABI addon) is a sub-decision of W16-2. Does NOT build automatic/continuous sync, does NOT write formats outside the v1 set, and does NOT rewrite audio stream bytes.
